DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
## What the paper argues

The paper proposes three things for 1 April:
- **Price rises** on three dishes: fish and chips £16.50 → £17.50, burger £15.00 → £16.00, sirloin £26.00 → £28.00. All three stay below the competitor midpoint.
- **Replacing the mushroom risotto**, which it says has the weakest margin and lowest sales, with a seasonal vegetarian special.
- **A projected gain** of £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in gross profit, lifting main-course margin to about 71%. It expects volumes to hold because guests are loyal.

I checked every figure against Table 1. The price increases look reasonable and well positioned against competitors. But two of the paper's central claims don't hold:
- **The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the lowest.**
- **The £42,000 projection ignores the 12% beef price rise** that the paper itself reports. It also probably overstates the gain by including VAT.

## What is sound

**Table 1 margins are calculated correctly.** Fish 69%, burger 72%, curry 75%, steak 60%, risotto 80%.

**The competitor positioning holds:**

| Dish | Competitor range | Midpoint | Proposed price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £16.95–£19.00 | £17.98 | £17.50 |
| Burger | £15.50–£17.50 | £16.50 | £16.00 |
| Steak | £27.00–£32.00 | £29.50 | £28.00 |

Each proposed price stays below the midpoint, as stated.

**The projection arithmetic is right on its own assumptions.** £310 + £260 + £240 = £810 a week, which is £42,120 a year. The "about 71%" margin also checks out: main-course margin goes from about 69.9% to about 71.3%, excluding specials, if costs don't change.

**The underlying case for a price review is sound.** Prices haven't changed since September 2024, and margin has slipped from 70% to 67%.

## 1. The risotto has the highest margin, not the weakest

| Dish | Margin | Gross profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80% (highest)** | **£11.20** |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |

- §5.2 and the author's description say the risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows the opposite. It has the best percentage margin, and it earns more per plate than the burger or the curry.
- **"Lowest sales" is a tie.** The risotto sells 90 a week, the same as specials.
- **Replacing it is likely to cost money.** Specials run at a 64% margin. A special at the same £14 price with that margin would cost about £5.04 to make, against the risotto's £2.80. That works out to:
  - about £200 a week less gross profit, at the same volume;
  - roughly £10,500 a year.
- This proposal works against the paper's goal of restoring margin. Unless there is another reason to drop the risotto, such as guest feedback, kitchen time or waste, the data say keep it.

## 2. The projection ignores the beef price rise

- §4 reports that beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same day as the new prices.
- §5.3 counts the full £1 burger increase and £2 steak increase as extra gross profit, with no change in food cost.
- **The worst case:** if the whole plate cost of the burger and steak rose 12%:
  - the burger would cost about £0.50 more;
  - the steak would cost about £1.25 more.

  That adds roughly **£280 a week** to costs.

| | Weekly |
|---|---|
| Paper's projection | £810 |
| Less beef cost rise (upper bound) | up to −£280 |
| Less risotto replacement | about −£200 |
| **Net** | **roughly £330–£530** |

- **The effect on margin:** with the beef rise, main-course margin ends up at about 69.7% rather than 71%, and lower again if the risotto is replaced. The "about 71%" holds only if costs stay where they are.
- **The real figure is likely somewhere in this range.** Beef is only part of each plate's cost, so £280 is an upper bound. The paper should cost the beef component of each dish.

## 3. VAT probably overstates both the margins and the projection

- In the UK, menu prices must include VAT, which is 20% for restaurant food. Gross profit is normally calculated on the price *excluding* VAT.
- Table 1 appears to calculate margins on the VAT-inclusive price. For example:
  - fish and chips at £16.50 is £13.75 net of VAT;
  - the margin on that is about 63%, not 69%.
- **The projection shrinks too.** A £1 price rise is about £0.83 net of VAT, so £810 a week becomes about **£675**, roughly £35,100 a year, before the beef cost.
- **Worth checking** how the 70% target is calculated. If it is net of VAT, as is standard, the restaurant is further below target than the paper suggests.

## 4. Monitoring will compare against a quiet season

- The eight-week monitoring compares spring sales with January–February.
- January and February are usually among the quietest months. Spring volumes may rise anyway, which could hide a fall in volume caused by the price rises.
- **Better comparisons:**
  - the same weeks last year;
  - each dish's *share* of total main courses, which separates price effects from overall trade.

## 5. Smaller points

- **Opening days:** §2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days. The Recommendation says "six trading days a week." The annual figure uses actual weekly sales, so it isn't affected, but the inconsistency should be fixed.
- **Repeat guests aren't necessarily price-insensitive.** 60% repeat bookings shows loyalty, but regulars are also the guests most likely to notice a rise. The 2024 increase passing without visible effect is reasonable but weak evidence.
- **Vegetarian option:** the replacement is a vegetarian special, so there is still a meat-free main. Worth making sure it is always available and not just occasional.

## What I'd ask the author to fix before the owners decide

1. Correct the risotto: it has the highest margin. Either keep it, or give a reason to remove it that isn't margin.
2. Cost the beef rise on the burger and steak, and restate the projection and margin net of it.
3. Confirm whether margins and the 70% target are calculated with or without VAT, and restate the figures consistently.
4. Monitor against the same weeks last year, or against each dish's share of sales, not against January–February.
5. Fix the trading days.

## Bottom line

The three price rises are sensible. They are modest, they keep the restaurant below competitors, and they are needed after 18 months without a change. But the real gain is likely to be roughly **£330–£530 a week**, not £810, once the beef cost and the risotto change are included, and less again net of VAT. Dropping the risotto would remove the highest-margin dish on the menu. Approve the price rises, keep the risotto, and ask for a corrected projection.
